messages.author: 3a775dfa0a96bf95
messages.subject: Combining colors
parts:
I would like to use color blending to represent overplotting of 2-3 different series more effectively.  Even where points are overplotted to the point where I can't distinguish the individual densities of point type A and point type B, I'd like to visualize the relative density of one or the other.

I've tried experimenting with the subtractive primaries (cyan, magenta, yellow) and alpha blending seems to do something moderately useful here (though yellow is visually much 'lighter' than the other two), but it's not great. I'd think that something like straight color addition (using additive primaries) instead of alpha-blending might give better results (with the sums renormalized to 1), but I don't really know.

Another problem with the alpha blending trick for single colors is that overplotting has an effective range of 0 to 1/alpha (linearly), which isn't very robust when some areas of the plot are much more heavily overplotted than others.  I wonder if there's some way to make this nonlinear (probit or log or whatever)....

Surely someone has thought about the use of color in overplotting more systematically?

         -s

messages.author: 3a775dfa0a96bf95
messages.subject: Re: Combining colors
parts:
Here are a couple of examples of what I have in mind:

clump <- function(x0=0,p=.5,n=500,prob=c(p,1-p),vdist=rexp)
  data.frame(x=runif(n,0,1)+x0,
             y=vdist(n),
             c=factor( sample(length(prob),n,prob=prob,replace=TRUE),
                       levels=1:length(prob),
                       ordered=TRUE ))

cc <- rbind(clump(0,0),clump(1,.4),clump(2,.2),clump(3,.6),clump(4,.4),clump(5,1))

dd <- rbind(clump(0,prob=c(.1,.3,.6)),
            clump(1,prob=c(.1,.6,.3)),
            clump(2,prob=c(.3,.1,.6)),
            clump(3,prob=c(.3,.6,.1)),
            clump(4,prob=c(.6,.1,.3)),
            clump(5,prob=c(.6,.3,.1)))

ee <- rbind(clump(0,0,vdist=runif),clump(1,.4,vdist=runif),clump(2,.2,vdist=runif),
            clump(3,.6,vdist=runif),clump(4,.4,vdist=runif),clump(5,1,vdist=runif))

test <- function(data) qplot(x,y,colour=c,data=data,size=I(5),alpha=I(.5))

Now try test(cc), test(dd), test(ee).

To a certain extent, you can see the different proportions through the color, but you have to look fairly hard.  I am imagining that there is some better way of combining colors so that the mixing proportions are more clearly visualized.

             -s

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: Combining colors
parts:
> To a certain extent, you can see the different proportions through the
> color, but you have to look fairly hard.  I am imagining that there is some
> better way of combining colors so that the mixing proportions are more
> clearly visualized.

I agree, but I'm not aware of anything in the literature.

To tackle this problem in general, it's probably best to do a 2d
density estimate yourself (on a common grid), and then compute and
visualise various quantities of interest. For example, plot f_a -
f_b, or f_a / (f_a + f_b).

Colour mixing will probably work for 2 or 3 colours, but it will
become increasingly hard to separate out the different colours.

I have some very preliminary ideas along these lines for a paper, but
I haven't made much progress.

Hadley

messages.author: 3a775dfa0a96bf95
messages.subject: Re: Combining colors
parts:
Agreed that 3 factor levels is probably the limit for this technique,
since the human visual system basically has 3 independent color
variables.

My own very preliminary idea would assign an additive primary (R, G,
B) to each level and have overplotting correspond to color addition,
with a final normalization step. Even better if the dots were fuzzy,
making it a sort of kernel relative density calculation.

-s
